tone_statements.quote: Difference also exists in the intonation pattern in words and phrases of a meaningful sentence observed in a proper context. The pitch rise and fall is more rough and unsteady within phrases in non-Musahars compared to Musahars. There is a steady and smooth falling pattern in the pitch curves in Musahars. A distinct differentiating feature found in the pitch pattern is that words begin with a high pitch in Musahars and start falling towards its end. The fall shows a smooth contour and is sometimes stepwise if one falling pitch line continues across a phrase containing more than one word.
tone_statements.locator: p. 155 (chapter 19, section following '2. Nomenclature of Musahars')
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone described or claimed; only a word/phrase-level high-then-falling intonational pitch contour noted as a sociophonetic marker of Bihar Musahar speech.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on pp.46-48 of Yadav 1996 in the page scan we hold (leaf26/leaf27); locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1996 Mouton reference grammar by the language's principal native-speaker phonetician, whose stress section condenses his 1984 phonology monograph (Yadav 1984 ch.5, downloaded now from archive.org). Yadav 1984 confirms every clause of our 'weight-hedged, right-edge, CVC + vowel-sequence final attracts stress, default penult' reading and refines it with counts (25% of disyllabic nominals final-stressed, all heavy-final; exceptions ['bahut], ['thehun]) and with an explicit statement that vowel length is nonphonemic, so 'CVV' in what counts as heavy: must be read as diphthong/vowel sequence, which the record's 'heavy' field already says. It also documents why StressTyp2/Hayes (from S. Jha 1958's length-based rules) disagrees - Yadav rejects that premise -

tone.quote: 2.15. Suprasegmental or Prosodic aspect: 2.16. Stress: Stress in Maithili is very soft and plays no important role. Sometimes it indicates topicality. Otherwise it is not clearly perceivable. Generally first syllable receives stress. ... But words of two syllables receive stress on the second if that is heavier: ... kəٰ ma:r / 'carpenter' ... In compounds second component is stressed: ... 2.17. Intonation: (i) Normal declarative sentences start with high pitch and end in low pitch ... (iii) Questions answerable with yes or no have rising pitch at the end ... 2.20. Juncture and pause: Juncture is a suprasegmental phoneme in almost all languages and Maithili is not exception.
tone.locator: web page, sections 2.15-2.17 and 2.20 (no printed pagination)
tone.summary: No lexical tone (implicit: prosody = weak stress + intonation + juncture).

tone.quote: p.1: 1. INTRODUCTION. Maithili, like most Indo-Aryan languages, is a stress language. However, stress in Maithi[l]i is far weaker than in English. ... Also, stress in Maithili is less significant. playing only a marginal role in distinguishing words ... p.6: Duration is a much more robust cue of word stress in Maithili than fundamental frequency since no particular pitch contour can be observed to correlate well with stress. For instance, the word pairs [giro] and [gi’ro] cannot be differentiated on grounds of pitch since no difference in pitch contour is observed on the narrow band spectrograms: both words have rising pitch on the first vowel followed by a falling pitch on the succeeding vowel.
